newsitem.title: USA: Bruno says NYS Senate may approve own NYC tax bill.
newsitem.headline: Bruno says NYS Senate may approve own NYC tax bill.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno (R-Troy) on Tuesday said that if the Assembly did not agree on a tax bill for New York City, the Senate likely would approve its own version and exit the special session.

The Senate Majority Leader explained that while he, Gov. George Pataki, and Mayor Rudolph Giuliani agreed that New York City's personal income tax surcharge should be extended for four years, the Assembly Speaker wanted a one-year extension.
Asked by reporters in Albany what he would do if there were no agreement, Bruno replied: "We'll do a one-houser and go home."
A one-houser is a term used to describe a bill that only has been approved by one house of the state legislature.

The state's top Democrat, Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver of Manhattan, earlier said that the bill to extend the city's tax levy, which is set to expire at year-end, had a chance to win approval, adding discussions were continuing.

He suggested that New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who had wanted more flexibility in spending the projected $455 million that the surcharge is expected to raise in the 1997 fiscal year, might be prepared to see more of the funds go toward increasing the police force, as the Speaker wanted.

"Well, the mayor has indicated that he's willing to live by some head count requirement," Silver said, explaining an acceptable variation from that total might range from one to two percent, though he felt the higher level was too much.
Press spokesmen for Giuliani had no information immediately available to comment.
Bruno said that while the dispute over the size of the police force had been one of the main stumbling blocks, that might be near resolution. "I think we're within range on that."

Further, Silver sugggested that the mayor and other top state and city officials might be willing to accept the Speaker's alternative proposal for a new borrowing authority for New York City, which would let it borrow up to $7.5 billion as a way of sidestepping its debt cap.

Silver said "We drafted a bill; the mayor has indicated that with some minor changes he would accept it; the governor has indicated he likes it; the budget directors indicated they like it; and Senator Bruno has indicated that what we have come up with addresses most of his concerns."
The Giuliani Administration had proposed setting up a new infrastructure authority, which the city comptroller had suggested could be allowed to borrow almost $11 billion.

Still, the speaker noted that there was at least one outstanding issue between the Assembly's proposal for a new agency and what the Senate would like to see. Silver said he knew of no precedent for the Senate to approve appointments to an authority made by the mayor, the city comptroller, or the speaker of the city council.

The Speaker appeared to raise the prospect of modifying how the city's debt limit is calculated, an issue he has suggested needed to be studied. The debt cap now is based on a five-year average of real estate values, but the sharp local recession in the early 1990s hurt the market and the cap does not fully reflect the rebound in this sector.

"Most other cities have a real estate property value as a cap because the real estate tax is the major source of their income. The City of New York has a personal income tax, which changes that equation compared to almost every other city in the state."
